nameStory: Meadowsweet gets its name from its sweet, honey-like fragrance and its love of damp meadows where it thrives. The 'sweet' also refers to its historical use in making mead, an alcoholic drink made from honey - hence its alternate name 'mead wort' where 'wort' is an old English word for plant.
description: Meadowsweet is a tall perennial herb that can reach 3-6 feet in height, creating impressive stands in wet areas. It produces frothy, cream-colored flower clusters that look like dollops of whipped cream sitting atop sturdy stems. The plant has a distinctly sweet, almond-like fragrance that's especially noticeable on warm, humid days. Its deeply divided leaves give it an elegant, feathery appearance that's easy to spot from a distance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, fluffy clusters of tiny cream or white flowers that smell sweetly of honey and almonds - crush a flower head gently between your fingers to release the intense fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 3-5 pairs of toothed leaflets plus a larger terminal leaflet, dark green on top with silvery-white undersides that flash in the breeze

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall upright stems that can tower 3-6 feet high, often growing in patches or colonies in consistently moist areas

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Reddish-purple stems that feel firm and hollow when gently squeezed, with a slight ridge running along their length

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small twisted seed pods that spiral like tiny corkscrews, clustered together where the flowers once bloomed

habitat: Look for meadowsweet in consistently moist to wet areas like streambanks, wet meadows, marsh edges, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in rich, organic soils and doesn't mind having its feet wet, often growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as reddish stems with unfurling compound leaves, growing rapidly in the warming weather.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August with intensely fragrant cream-colored flower clusters that attract numerous pollinators including bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed clusters while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, though the sweet fragrance can still linger in dried flower heads.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving only dried brown stems and seed heads that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Meadowsweet contains the same active compound (salicin) that aspirin is made from - in fact, the original aspirin was first synthesized from this very plant in 1838, making it one of our most important medicinal discoveries hiding in plain sight in wet meadows!
confusionNotes: Meadowsweet's fluffy white flower clusters might remind you of elderflower, but elderflower grows on woody shrubs while meadowsweet is an herb with hollow reddish stems. Remember: if it smells like sweet almonds and has reddish stems in a wet area, it's meadowsweet.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'meadowsweet,' this plant is actually not native to New England - it was introduced from Europe and has naturalized here. Many of its common names like 'queen of the meadow' and 'bridewort' reflect its long history of use in European folk medicine and wedding ceremonies.
compareHints: Meadowsweet is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, though you might occasionally encounter queen of the prairie which has pink flowers instead of white. Both share that distinctive sweet fragrance, but queen of the prairie prefers slightly drier conditions and is much less common in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Queen of the prairie stands out from its meadowsweet cousins by its pink flowers and taller stature - meadowsweet has white or cream flowers and typically grows shorter.
Dropwort is much smaller and more delicate than its cousin meadowsweet, with finer, more divided leaves and smaller flower clusters.
Giant meadowsweet dwarfs its relatives - regular meadowsweet typically grows 3-4 feet tall with smaller flower clusters, while queen of the prairie has pink flowers instead of white.
